ann_23.text: Through this part, which reads a4 and a5, giving a4 its first value slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' if a5 = 4, but the other way if a5 = 1, with the typical case staying below 1% (on the training data only).

ann_24.text: Through this part, moving a1, a3, a5 or a6 away from its first value slightly raises the typical case's predicted probability of 'yes', and giving a2 its first value slightly lowers it, all staying below 1%.
Giving a4 its first value slightly lowers it as well (on the training data only).

ann_25.text: This part of the model acts on 92 of the 345 training cases, and 3 of those 92 are actually 'yes'.
For the typical case it acts on (a1 = 2, a2 = 3, a3 = 2, a4 = 2, a5 = 4, a6 = 2), it clearly moves the predicted probability of 'yes' from above 99% without the part to below 1% with it.

For the typical case with a1 other than 1, changing a6 from 1 to 2 clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to about 77%, and with a3 = 2, to about 68%, while with a1 = 1 or a3 = 1 it stays below 1%.

Through this part, for the typical case it acts on, moving a3 or a6 away from its first value slightly lowers the predicted probability of 'yes', and changing a2 from 3 to 1 or to 2 slightly raises it, all staying below 1%.
Moving a1 away from its first value slightly lowers it too (on the training data only).
The effects of a6 and a4 through this part also depend slightly on a2 and a6.

ann_26.text: The model as a whole clearly predicts 'yes' when exactly two of the six attributes take their first value, and 'no' when none, one, or three or more do.
Among training cases, 110 of the 113 with exactly two get 'yes' and none of the others do, and it follows the rule on 86 of the 87 test cases.
On average the predicted probability of 'yes' is about 1% for training cases at the counts predicted 'no' and about 78% for cases with exactly two.
For the typical case, changing a2 from 3 to 2 slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes', which stays below 1%.

ann_23.original: A4/a5 first-value pool (with an inert a4:2 sub-unit). Write I_k for 'attribute k takes its first value'. In indicator form node 389 = ReLU(-0.744 + 3.793 I4 + 3.317 I5 + 0.492 [a5=4] - 0.0006 u), where u = node 2443 = ReLU(0.997 [a4=2] - 1.281) is identically zero on the whole domain (maximum pre-activation -0.284), so the a4:2 branch is inert (and its readout weight is -0.0006 anyway). With neither a4 nor a5 at its first value the pool outputs 0 (pre-activation -0.744 or -0.252); a4=1 alone gives 3.05 (3.54 when a5=4), a5=1 alone gives 2.57, both give 6.37. The pool is therefore a rectified, near-additive count of the two rule indicators I4 and I5, which the downstream gate does not receive directly. EVIDENCE: Train split (n=345, full sample): node 2443 is 0 on every row; sensitivity of the pool to a4:2 is 0.0, to a4:1 0.86, a5:1 0.71, a5:4 0.10. The pool takes exactly five values on train: 0 (176 rows), 2.573 (a5=1, 62), 3.049 (a4=1, 57), 3.541 (a4=1, a5=4, 25), 6.366 (a4=1 and a5=1, 25).
ann_23.proposed: A small pool of a4 and a5 whose a4 effect slightly reverses with a5 (on the training data only).

ann_24.original: Linear descending count ramp. In indicator form the direct input-to-output connections sum to 16.73 - 8.89 I1 - 8.08 I2 - 8.41 I3 - 1.66 I4 - 6.19 I5 - 8.73 I6 (exact; a6 enters through its complement a6:2 with +8.73, the same signal inverted). Every first-value indicator lowers the score by 6 to 9, except I4 (-1.66), whose shortfall is made up at the root by the pool readout (-0.888 x Pool, i.e. about -2.7 for I4 and -2.3 for I5). The ramp falls approximately linearly with the number of active rule indicators. EVIDENCE: Train split (n=345, full sample): sensitivities equal the absolute weights (a1:1 4.25, a2:1 3.82, a3:1 4.20, a4:1 0.77, a5:1 2.69, a6:2 4.36), as expected for a linear map. Indicator-form least squares fit over all 432 configurations is exact (residual 5.5e-14): 16.73 - 8.89 I1 - 8.08 I2 - 8.41 I3 - 1.66 I4 - 6.19 I5 - 8.73 I6.
ann_24.proposed: A linear score that slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' when a1, a3, a5 or a6 moves away from its first value and slightly lowers it when a2 or a4 takes its first value.

ann_25.original: Low-count veto gate, a serial composition Veto(a1, a2, a3, a6, Pool(a4, a5)). Node 288 = ReLU(17.125 - 10.71 I1 - 7.81 I2 + 0.74 [a2=3] - 9.85 I3 - 11.82 I6 - 3.378 Pool). Through the pool, I4 alone subtracts 10.3 (12.0 when a5=4), I5 alone 8.7, both 21.5. Every active first-value indicator thus removes 7.8 to 11.8 from a bias of 17.1: the gate is on (5.16 to 17.87) for every configuration with zero or one active indicators and off for two or more, with one exception: I2 + I5 (a2=1 and a5=1) leaves 17.125 - 7.81 - 8.69 = 0.62 > 0, a small leak. So 288 detects 'at most one of the six rule indicators is active'. EVIDENCE: Train split (n=345, full sample), by number of active first-value indicators: count 0 (19 rows) gate 17.13..17.87, on 100%; count 1 (70) gate 5.16..9.32, on 100%; count 2 (113) on 2.7% (3 rows, all a2=1 and a5=1, value 0.62); count >=3 (143) off 100%. Sensitivities: a6:1 1.58, a1:1 1.37, a3:1 1.31, a2:1 0.98, pool 0.90, a2:3 0.09. Over all 432 configurations the same pattern holds (on for count <=1; on at count 2 only for the 4 a2=1,a5=1 configurations).
ann_25.proposed: This part acts on 92 training cases, 3 of them actually 'yes', and pushes their predicted probability of 'yes' from above 99% to below 1%; with it, changing a6 from 1 to 2 turns the typical case to 'yes' when a1 is other than 1 or a3 = 2.

ann_26.original: Exactly-two window = descending ramp minus low-count veto. Output = sigmoid(1.383 + Ramp - 4.009 Veto - 0.888 Pool). The linear part (bias + ramp + pool readout) by number of active first-value indicators: 0 -> 18.1, 1 -> 9.2 to 13.8, 2 -> 0.49 to 5.67, 3 -> -8.0 to -2.75, 4 or more -> below -11.5; it is positive iff at most two indicators are active (upper edge of the window). The veto is at least 5.16 whenever at most one indicator is active, so -4.009 Veto <= -20.7 overrides the ramp's maximum of 18.1 (lower edge). The output is therefore above 0.5 exactly when two indicators are active, with one exception: for count two made of a2=1 and a5=1, the veto leaks 0.62, and 0.62 x 4.009 = 2.49 exceeds the ramp margin 1.56 (pre-activation -0.93), so the 4 such configurations (a1 in {2,3}, a2=1, a3=2, a4 in {2,3}, a5=1, a6=2) are scored negative. The inputs a1:2, a1:3, a2:2, a3:2, a4:3, a5:2, a5:3 have no enabled connections and zero effect; they are listed here as zero-effect entry nodes. EVIDENCE: Train split (n=345, full sample): accuracy 0.991, AUC 1.000. Linear part (bias + ramp - 0.888 pool) per count: 0 -> 18.11; 1 -> 9.22..13.75; 2 -> 0.49..5.67; 3 -> -7.98..-2.75; 4 -> -16.39..-11.48; 5 -> -24.48..-20.37; 6 -> -29.50. Output > 0.5 for 0% of count 0/1/3/4/5/6 rows and 97.3% of count 2 rows; the 3 misses are the a2=1,a5=1 veto leak (output 0.283). Sensitivity of the output: veto 0.213, ramp 0.053, pool 0.047, all seven unconnected inputs 0.0. Over all 432 configurations the network agrees with 'exactly two indicators' on 428 (the 4 a2=1,a5=1 count-2 configurations are the only disagreements).
ann_26.proposed: The model predicts 'yes' when exactly two of the six attributes take their first value and 'no' otherwise, on 110 of 113 training cases with exactly two, every other training case and 86 of 87 test cases.

summary.text: The model clearly predicts 'yes' when exactly two of the six attributes take their first value (a1 = 1, a2 = 1 and so on), and 'no' at every other count: 110 of the 113 training cases with exactly two get 'yes', and none of the other training cases do.

It follows this rule on 86 of the 87 test cases, and on average the predicted probability of 'yes' is about 1% for training cases at the counts predicted 'no' and about 78% for cases with exactly two.

The typical case has the most common value of each attribute (a1 = 1, a2 = 3, a3 = 1, a4 = 2, a5 = 1, a6 = 1); with a1 other than 1 instead, changing a6 from 1 to 2 clearly raises the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to about 77%, and with a3 = 2 instead, to about 68%, while with a1 = 1 and a3 = 1 it stays below 1%.
One part of the model acts on 92 of the 345 training cases, and 3 of those 92 are actually 'yes'.
For the typical case this part acts on, which has no attribute at its first value, it clearly moves the predicted probability of 'yes' from above 99% without the part to below 1% with it.
For the typical case, changing a2 from 3 to 2 slightly raises the predicted probability of 'yes', which stays below 1%.

Linear part (bias + ramp - 0.888 pool) per count: 0 -> 18.11; 1 -> 9.22..13.75; 2 -> 0.49..5.67; 3 -> -7.98..-2.75; 4 -> -16.39..-11.48; 5 -> -24.48..-20.37; 6 -> -29.50. Output > 0.5 for 0% of count 0/1/3/4/5/6 rows and 97.3% of count 2 rows; the 3 misses are the a2=1,a5=1 veto leak (output 0.283). Sensitivity of the output: veto 0.213, ramp 0.053, pool 0.047, all seven unconnected inputs 0.0. Over all 432 configurations the network agrees with 'exactly two indicators' on 428 (the 4 a2=1,a5=1 count-2 configurations are the only disagreements).

parts.name: low_count_veto_gate
parts.original_hypothesis: Low-count veto gate, a serial composition Veto(a1, a2, a3, a6, Pool(a4, a5)). Node 288 = ReLU(17.125 - 10.71 I1 - 7.81 I2 + 0.74 [a2=3] - 9.85 I3 - 11.82 I6 - 3.378 Pool). Through the pool, I4 alone subtracts 10.3 (12.0 when a5=4), I5 alone 8.7, both 21.5. Every active first-value indicator thus removes 7.8 to 11.8 from a bias of 17.1: the gate is on (5.16 to 17.87) for every configuration with zero or one active indicators and off for two or more, with one exception: I2 + I5 (a2=1 and a5=1) leaves 17.125 - 7.81 - 8.69 = 0.62 > 0, a small leak. So 288 detects 'at most one of the six rule indicators is active'. EVIDENCE: Train split (n=345, full sample), by number of active first-value indicators: count 0 (19 rows) gate 17.13..17.87, on 100%; count 1 (70) gate 5.16..9.32, on 100%; count 2 (113) on 2.7% (3 rows, all a2=1 and a5=1, value 0.62); count >=3 (143) off 100%. Sensitivities: a6:1 1.58, a1:1 1.37, a3:1 1.31, a2:1 0.98, pool 0.90, a2:3 0.09. Over all 432 configurations the same pattern holds (on for count <=1; on at count 2 only for the 4 a2=1,a5=1 configurations).

parts.name: a4_a5_first_value_pool
parts.original_hypothesis: A4/a5 first-value pool (with an inert a4:2 sub-unit). Write I_k for 'attribute k takes its first value'. In indicator form node 389 = ReLU(-0.744 + 3.793 I4 + 3.317 I5 + 0.492 [a5=4] - 0.0006 u), where u = node 2443 = ReLU(0.997 [a4=2] - 1.281) is identically zero on the whole domain (maximum pre-activation -0.284), so the a4:2 branch is inert (and its readout weight is -0.0006 anyway). With neither a4 nor a5 at its first value the pool outputs 0 (pre-activation -0.744 or -0.252); a4=1 alone gives 3.05 (3.54 when a5=4), a5=1 alone gives 2.57, both give 6.37. The pool is therefore a rectified, near-additive count of the two rule indicators I4 and I5, which the downstream gate does not receive directly. EVIDENCE: Train split (n=345, full sample): node 2443 is 0 on every row; sensitivity of the pool to a4:2 is 0.0, to a4:1 0.86, a5:1 0.71, a5:4 0.10. The pool takes exactly five values on train: 0 (176 rows), 2.573 (a5=1, 62), 3.049 (a4=1, 57), 3.541 (a4=1, a5=4, 25), 6.366 (a4=1 and a5=1, 25).

parts.name: linear_count_ramp
parts.original_hypothesis: Linear descending count ramp. In indicator form the direct input-to-output connections sum to 16.73 - 8.89 I1 - 8.08 I2 - 8.41 I3 - 1.66 I4 - 6.19 I5 - 8.73 I6 (exact; a6 enters through its complement a6:2 with +8.73, the same signal inverted). Every first-value indicator lowers the score by 6 to 9, except I4 (-1.66), whose shortfall is made up at the root by the pool readout (-0.888 x Pool, i.e. about -2.7 for I4 and -2.3 for I5). The ramp falls approximately linearly with the number of active rule indicators. EVIDENCE: Train split (n=345, full sample): sensitivities equal the absolute weights (a1:1 4.25, a2:1 3.82, a3:1 4.20, a4:1 0.77, a5:1 2.69, a6:2 4.36), as expected for a linear map. Indicator-form least squares fit over all 432 configurations is exact (residual 5.5e-14): 16.73 - 8.89 I1 - 8.08 I2 - 8.41 I3 - 1.66 I4 - 6.19 I5 - 8.73 I6.

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

summary.text: The model clearly predicts 'yes' when exactly two of the attributes take their first value, and otherwise not (at every count, at least 97% of the training cases get the same prediction).

For a typical case, going from a6 = 1 to a6 = 2 moves the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to about 77% if attribute a1 is something other than a1 = 1, and from below 1% to below 1% if a1 = 1.

This changes the prediction only slightly: for a typical case, going from a4 = 2 to a4 = 1 moves the predicted probability of 'yes' from below 1% to below 1% if a6 = 2, and from below 1% to below 1% if a6 = 1.
